column1: # 80 primary URLs across nine strata, plus a marked reserve block used only
# to replace a primary that fails. Collected by scripts/collect.py into
#   url                a page, not a homepage, except where the risk column
#                      says `homepage` and the reason says why
#   stratum            one of the nine; every figure is reported per stratum
#   risk               what is most likely to go wrong with this row:
#                        ok             expected to fetch and parse
#                        rot            deep URL, may have moved since it
#                        robots         robots.txt may disallow this path
#   selection_reason   why THIS url, in one line
# The risk column is a prediction, not a result. What actually happened is
# in collection.json, and every report's denominator is URLs ATTEMPTED (80),
# UNVERIFIED: no URL below has been fetched. Deep article paths are written
# from memory against a May 2026 cutoff and today is 2026-08-29, so the `rot`
# rows are the ones expected to fail. That is what the 60-page floor is for.
# news / magazine -- 10.  Floated figures, pull quotes, ad slots, multi-column
# teasers. The stratum where CSS 2.1 chapter 9 floats should be densest.

column4: Major broadcaster section page; server-rendered shell with heavy progressive enhancement, so it measures the common "SSR plus hydration" shape
Section page mixing a card grid with article teasers; no hard paywall, and long-lived CSS with a documented design system
NPR's deliberately text-only edition -- the near-zero-CSS extreme of this stratum, and a control for what a news page costs without layout
Long-form with floated figures and inline ad slots; the classic float-heavy article body
Wire service hub page; plain structural markup, few tables, good baseline
International outlet whose Arabic sibling appears in the non-Latin stratum, giving one organisation across two scripts
Public broadcaster with older CSS than the US/UK majors; expected to be more table- and float-reliant
Long-form science with SVG figures, pull quotes and a distinctive editorial layout
Magazine section page; image-grid heavy, expected to be flex-dense for a news site
Investigative long-form; graphics-heavy bodies and a nonprofit-newsroom stylesheet rather than a commercial CMS

column1: # documentation / reference -- 10.  Long flow content, tables, <pre>, sidebars.
# Row 9 is a deliberate CONTROL, see below.

column4: MDN's page for the shorthand Task F implemented: syntax tables, code blocks, a sticky sidebar, and on-topic for the flex census
One of the largest Sphinx pages on the web; dozens of tables and a deep heading tree, which stresses table layout on real markup
Dense multi-column reference tables with wrapping cells -- the shape chapter 17's fixed/auto width algorithms actually meet
mdBook output: minimal hand-written CSS, a flex sidebar, and long <pre> blocks with no wrapping
Long single-page flow with admonition boxes and inline code; a different documentation generator from the other four
A man page as HTML: almost entirely <pre>, essentially no author CSS, the low-CSS floor for this stratum
HTTP semantics as a very long preformatted document; tests white-space:pre handling and intrinsic sizing at extreme length
The visual formatting model chapter this engine implements, in W3C's own 1998-era stylesheet
CONTROL: the identical URL already in the 2026-08-27-phase-3 collection. Two fetch dates for one page separates "the page changed" from "the engine changed" -- the only row here that can do that
Hugo-built docs with a modern three-column flex shell, contrasting with the four older generators above

column1: # e-commerce -- 10.  Product grids are the densest flex on the web. This is
# also the RISKIEST stratum: bot protection and robots.txt disallow are both
# routine here, and it is the one most likely to fall short of 10.

column4: Independent electronics retailer with a bot-tolerant robots.txt; a real product page with gallery, variant selector and spec table
Same category as Adafruit with a different template; product IDs churn, so this row is expected to need replacement
Shopify-hosted category grid -- Shopify's default templates are among the most-deployed flex layouts anywhere
Open storefront with a dense responsive card grid and no bot protection; the cleanest large product grid likely to fetch
Large commercial storefront that still server-renders its product pages; heavy nested flex in the purchase modules
Print-on-demand search results: a paginated grid with query-string URLs, which also exercises the slug fix
Independent bookseller aggregator; list pages are grid-heavy and the site is small enough to be politely fetched
Large US retailer category page with faceted navigation; included knowing bot protection may refuse it, because the stratum needs at least one big-retailer template
Category grid from a retailer whose layout is almost entirely flex and grid; likely client-rendered, which is itself the finding
Second big-retailer template so the stratum does not rest on one; expected to be the second most likely refusal

column1: # SPA shells -- 8.  Near-empty DOM. These are a FINDING, not a failure: a
# page that parses to 15 elements and lays out nothing is a fact about the
# web, and excluding it is the selection bias this sample exists to escape.

column4: Canvas-based drawing app; the document is a mount point and essentially all layout is client-side
Second canvas app with a different bundler and framework, so the stratum is not one toolchain
The RealWorld reference SPA -- a deliberately conventional React app, the median of this stratum rather than an extreme
TodoMVC's React example: the smallest honest SPA on the web, and a useful floor for "how few elements does a page have"
Framework-authored playground; Angular's shell markup differs structurally from React's
Svelte compiles away its framework, so its shell is closer to hand-written HTML than the others -- a contrast within the stratum
Notebook runtime: content is generated entirely after load, and the served document is near-empty
Long-lived, non-venture-backed web app; an older SPA idiom than the framework demos above

column1: # government / public sector -- 10.  Old markup, tables used for layout, CSS
# written under procurement. Expected to be the highest table-layout density
# in the sample and a strong test of chapter 17 on markup nobody validated.

column4: GDS design system: modern, accessible, deliberately plain CSS -- the well-engineered end of this stratum
US federal forms index; dense data tables and a legacy CMS
Public health content with heavy internal cross-linking; recently reorganised, so the path may have moved
A long alphabetical index; the simplest possible structural page at real length
Bilingual federal service page on a shared national template
EU institutional page; multilingual infrastructure and a cookie banner that may or may not replace the document
Federal judiciary; older markup than the executive-branch sites above
Statistical agency: data tables are the content rather than the chrome
Large municipal site -- the layer where table-based layout genuinely survives, and the reason this stratum is 10 and not 6
Second large municipal site on a different vendor CMS, so the municipal finding is not one procurement

column1: # personal sites / blogs -- 10.  Hand-written HTML and minimal CSS at one end,
# elaborate typographic CSS at the other. Chosen as a deliberate RANGE: rows 1
# and 5 are close to the minimum and maximum author-CSS budgets on the web.

column4: Famously near-zero CSS: no stylesheet worth the name, so almost every computed value is our UA sheet -- the floor of the author/UA gap
The opposite extreme: floated sidenotes, drop caps, multi-column and a very large hand-tuned stylesheet
Hand-written posts with inline SVG and code blocks; a specific post URL, so rot-prone
A tag index rather than a post, which is more stable and still a real content page
Hugo-generated, deliberately plain; represents the static-site-generator default that thousands of blogs ship unchanged
Written by a CSS layout spec editor, so the page itself is likely to use grid and flex correctly and idiomatically
Long-running blog by the author of the CSS reset; markup and CSS with two decades of accumulated layers
Progressive-enhancement advocate; expected to degrade unusually well and to use very little JS
Deliberately minimal by stated policy -- a second low-CSS row so the danluu finding is not a single site
Elaborate custom typography and a hand-rolled layout; homepage because the site's index is its content

column1: # forums / community -- 8.  Deep nesting, query-string URLs, and the last
# genuine table-layout holdouts. Two rows are chosen specifically to exercise
# the slug fix (query strings), which three hand-picked URLs never could.

column4: An early, permanently-present HN item, and a QUERY-STRING url -- the exact shape that silently collided before the slug fix. Same domain as the phase-3 collection but a different page type
Small hand-written community site; table-based listing markup with almost no framework CSS
Discourse is a client-rendered forum with a virtual scroller -- likely a near-empty document, which makes it an SPA finding inside the forum stratum
phpBB with a query-string url: nested tables, decades-old markup idioms, and a second slug-fix exercise
vBulletin-era layout; the most likely row in the sample to use tables for page structure rather than data
Mailing list archive: nested <ul> threading and <pre> bodies, essentially no CSS at all
Reddit's legacy interface, which is table- and float-based; robots.txt is restrictive and this row is expected to be refused
Q&A tag page with dense code blocks and vote widgets; bot protection is likely and the row is included knowing it

column1: # marketing / landing -- 8.  MY ADDITION, and the highest-yield eight slots
# for moving register rows off zero. The hero/feature-grid/pricing-table idiom
# is where flex-direction:column, order, align-content and multi-line wrapping
# actually live. Rows 4 and 5 are PRICING PAGES, chosen specifically for
# column-direction flex, which has zero occurrences in the current corpus.

column4: The most-imitated marketing layout on the web; gradients, layered absolute positioning and deeply nested flex
Feature grid with staggered cards; a current-generation design-system landing page
Built by the authors of the utility framework most responsible for how much flex is on the web; near-certain to exercise wrap and gap
PRICING PAGE: side-by-side plan cards are column-direction flex with wrapping, the single most likely source of a non-zero flex-direction:column count
Second pricing page on a different design system, so a column-flex finding is not one site
Product page as layout showcase; sticky headers, staged reveals and very heavy nesting
Deliberately plain, opinionated marketing with hand-written CSS -- the low-complexity control for this stratum
Visual-builder output: machine-generated CSS with a distinctive class naming scheme, structurally unlike hand-authored pages

column1: # non-Latin script -- 6.  MY ADDITION, with the caveat stated: the vendored
# Liberation Sans covers none of these scripts, so these pages produce
# MISSING-GLYPH and SCRIPT-CLASSIFICATION counts, not box positions to trust.
# Six writing systems, two right-to-left. `characters classified AL by
# default: must be 0` cannot be tested by any other row in this file.

column4: Japanese: no inter-word spaces, mixed kanji/kana/Latin runs, and full-width punctuation with its own line-break rules
Traditional Chinese: Han-only runs with no spaces, and a query-free listing page that should fetch cleanly
Arabic: RIGHT-TO-LEFT with cursive joining. This engine has no bidi at all, so the finding is how loudly that fails and what it counts
Hebrew: the second RTL script, non-joining, so RTL and cursive-joining failures can be told apart rather than confounded
Thai: NO INTER-WORD SPACES AT ALL and no ASCII fallback, which is the sharpest possible test of line breaking -- there is literally nothing to break on
Devanagari: combining marks and reordering vowels, where a naive per-codepoint measurement diverges from grapheme clusters
